title: The Plating Workshop
story: You and NOVA are in an electroplating workshop when the safety doors close. NOVA is learning how electric current changes liquids. Help it get things right to open the doors.
escaped: The doors open. NOVA now knows which liquids conduct, why electroplating is used and how a weak current can fool a test.

locks.title: Will it conduct?
locks.intro: NOVA must sort liquids into those that conduct electricity and those that don't. Choose its clues.

features.text: Has salts, acids or bases dissolved in it

locks.hint: Tap water and distilled water both look clear. What does tap water have in it that distilled water doesn't?
locks.learn: How a liquid looks or where it's used doesn't decide whether it conducts. Dissolved salts, acids or bases do, which is why tap water conducts and distilled water hardly does.

locks.title: Fix NOVA's electroplating notes
locks.intro: NOVA has notes on why things are electroplated. Tick the wrong ones.

rows.label: Gives a shiny finish that doesn't scratch easily
Tin is less reactive, so food doesn't spoil

rows.item: Gold or silver on cheap jewellery
rows.label: Makes it look like gold or silver
Used because chromium is cheap
rows.why: chromium is expensive, so only a thin layer is put on a cheaper metal

locks.hint: Why is only a THIN layer of chromium used?
locks.learn: Wrong 'reasons' in training data teach an AI to explain things wrongly, even when its answer sounds smooth.

locks.title: Check NOVA's experiment report
locks.intro: NOVA wrote up an experiment. Is it right? Decide and pick the fact that settles it.
locks.claim: Passing electricity through water does nothing to it.
evidence: When current passes through water with a little salt, bubbles of oxygen and hydrogen form at the electrodes.
An LED glows even with a weak current.
Distilled water is a poor conductor.
locks.hint: What appears at the electrodes during the experiment?
locks.learn: 'Nothing happened' is a claim too, and it needs checking. Careful observation (the bubbles) is the evidence that decides.

locks.title: Bulb or LED?
locks.intro: NOVA tested liquids with two testers: one with a bulb and one with an LED.
locks.question: NOVA says: 'The bulb didn't glow in lemon juice, so lemon juice doesn't conduct.' What is the honest conclusion?
options: NOVA is right: no glow means no current.
Lemon juice conducts a little: the current was too weak for the bulb but enough for the LED.
locks.hint: Which tester works with a smaller current?
locks.learn: A test can miss something real if it isn't sensitive enough. An AI trained only on bulb-tester results would learn that lemon juice doesn't conduct, which is wrong.
